title: Hoobastank, Simple Plan and More Bands Performed Mid-Flight During Nationwide Air Travel Ground Stop
description: Southwest Airlines brought back its “Live at 35” program during Friday’s nationwide grounding of air travel with performances from artists on their
body:
Southwest Airlines brought back its “Live at 35” program during Friday’s nationwide grounding of air travel with performances from artists on their way to Vans Warped Tour.

	Hoobastank, The Used, Simple Plan and Lolo performed aboard a Southwest flight from Los Angeles to Orlando, Fla., on Nov. 13 as part of the music program, which hosts surprise midflight pop-up performances. The flight left Los Angeles around 11 a.m., about two hours before the FAA declared a national ground stop that snarled global travel and left more than 1 million people stranded.
	

	Hoobastank took to the aisles at cruising altitude for a live rendition of their 2004 hit “The Reason.” Passengers sang along and posted about the performance on social media. Lolo, who played at Warped Tour’s Long Beach, Calif., stop in July, wrote “Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew.”

	The sky-high performance came amid a nationwide ground stop for all flights, with the Federal Aviation Administration citing “extraordinary circumstances.” The initial alert came just after 1 p.m. PT on Friday, stranding some 1.5 million travelers by CNN’s estimate. Airborne flights were allowed to continue, but new domestic flights were delayed or canceled, throwing travel plans into question for various industry events over the weekend. The stop was lifted about five hours later, shortly before 6 p.m. PT.

	The “Live at 35” artists were in route to the final Vans Warped Tour 2026 stop in Orlando, which runs Nov. 14-15 at Camping World Stadium Campus. The Warped Tour expanded from three to five locations in 2026, with two-day festivals in Washington, D.C., Long Beach and Orlando, Fla. alongside two new international sites in Montreal, Canada and Mexico City.
	

	Founded in 1995, Vans Warped Tour has become a definitive rock and alt festival, featuring 100+ artists across rock, pop punk, alternative, emo and more genres. Past performers include Blink-182, No Doubt, Sublime, Beck, Katy Perry, NOFX, Limp Bizkit, Black Eyed Peas, Green Day, Eminem, Yellowcard, Bad Religion and more.

title: Adam Driver Says Disney Killing ‘The Hunt for Ben Solo’ Felt ‘Criminal’: ‘Steven Soderbergh Wants to Make a “Star Wars” Movie. What Are We Debating?’
description: Adam Driver continues to express his dissatisfaction with Disney over the decision to kill his “Star Wars” sequel movie “The Hunt for Ben Solo,” wh
body:
Adam Driver continues to express his dissatisfaction with Disney over the decision to kill his “Star Wars” sequel movie “The Hunt for Ben Solo,” which he spent two-and-a-half years developing with director Steven Soderbergh. In a new interview with The Associated Press on his “Paper Tiger” press tour, the Oscar nominee said he was surprised Soderbergh’s involvement alone didn’t have the studio jumping at the chance to make the movie.
	

	“For me it was: Steven Soderbergh wants to make a ‘Star Wars’ film. What are we debating?” Driver said. “It’s what it is. It’s criminal. Or it felt criminal. We’re all moving on. On to the next. And Steven already has something else that’s one of the best things he’s ever written.”


	Driver revealed the existence of “The Hunt for Ben Solo” in an Oct. 2025 interview with The Associated Press, explaining how Disney executives pulled the plug on the project because they couldn’t wrap their heads around the character coming back after he presumably died in 2019’s “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker.”

	“I always was interested in doing another ‘Star Wars,’” Driver said at the time. “I had been talking about doing another one since 2021. Kathleen [Kennedy] had reached out. I always said: ‘With a great director and a great story, I’d be there in a second.’ I loved that character and loved playing him.”

	The mere existence of “The Hunt for Ben Solo” instantly mobilized “Star Wars” fans on social media into calling for Disney to reverse its decision and put the “Star Wars” project back in development. A group of “Star Wars” fans even paid for a plane to fly a banner reading “Save ‘The Hunt for Ben Solo’” over Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, Calif. Even Daisy Ridley, who starred opposite Driver as Rey in the most “Star Wars” sequel trilogy, championed fans for their support of “The Hunt for Ben Solo.”
	

	“I was blown away by the response to it,” Driver told the AP in his latest interview. “In no way did I think there would be billboards in Times Square. It’s so moving. It did feel like we were all at the bar having a conversation about the films we wanted to see.”

	Earlier in his “Paper Tiger” press tour, Driver said on “The Rich Eisen Show” that his time playing Kylo Ren/Ben Solo is officially over now that “The Hunt for Ben Solo” is dead and gone. The actor said: “If they wanted to, fine. But we’re not … It’s not our call. I think the ship has sailed though.”

title: Skip Hinnant, ‘The Electric Company’ Actor and Voice of Ralph Bakshi’s ‘Fritz the Cat’ Movies, Dies at 86
description: Actor Skip Hinnant, best known for his work on the PBS children’s series “The Electric Company‘ and as the voice of Fritz the Cat in Ralph Bakshi’s
body:
Actor Skip Hinnant, best known for his work on the PBS children’s series “The Electric Company‘ and as the voice of Fritz the Cat in Ralph Bakshi’s racy animated films from the 1970s, has died. He was 86.

	Hinnant’s death was confirmed by his family in an obituary notice published by the New York Times. He died Nov. 8 in Denver.

	Hinnant was active in theater in the 1960s. He originated the role of Schroeder in the Off Broadway debut of Peanuts musical “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown” in 1967. He was part of the renowned Julius Monk revue “Struts and Frets” in 1963. The previous year, Hinnant had a recurring role on the popular ABC sitcom “The Patty Duke Show.” He appeared at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner in 1962, performing for President John F. Kennedy.
	

	Hinnant’s other credits include voicing the Easter Bunny in the 1977 Rankin-Bass animated TV special “The Easter Bunny is Comin’ to Town,” which was narrated by Fred Astaire. In later years, his credits included “Kate & Allie,” “As the World Turns,” “3 2 1 Contact.” 

	Hinnant was prolific in voice-over work in animation and TV commercials. He was also known for his active involvement with Actors Equity, AFTRA and SAG (before the latter unions merged) from the 1980s through the early 2000s.

	Born Joseph Howard Hinnant in 1940, he grew up in Chincoteague Island, Virginia. He was nicknamed Skip by his older sister Jean. The name stuck as his acting career blossomed. 

	Hinnant was a charter member in 1971 of the cast of PBS’ “The Electric Company,” a companion daytime series to “Sesame Street” that sought to help older kids develop critical thinking skills. He stayed with the series through its end in 1977, playing a range of characters per the fast-paced, sketch-centered format. Fellow cast members over the years included Rita Moreno, Morgan Freeman, Zero Mostel and Bill Cosby.
	

	During the run of “The Electric Company,” Hinnant was recruited by legendary animator Ralph Bakshi to voice the title character in 1972’s “Fritz the Cat,” based on the lascivious stoner cat character created by Robert Crumb. The film was underground hit — despite Crumb’s objection to the film adaptation — and yielded a 1974 follow up, “The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat.”

	Hinnant attended Yale University, graduating in 1962. 

	He is survived by his first wife, Miriam Hinnant, his longtime companion Ruth Nerken, four children and nine grandchildren. The family requests that donations be made in Hinnant’s name to the Entertainment Community Fund or the SAG-AFTRA Foundation.

	(Pictured: Skip Hinnant and Rita Moreno on “The Electric Company”)

title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Stars Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy on Playing Sisters With Secrets and That Twisty Killer Ending
description:
Nov 14, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
	‘The Good Daughter’ Stars Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy on Playing Sisters With Secrets and That Twisty Killer En
body:
Nov 14, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
	‘The Good Daughter’ Stars Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy on Playing Sisters With Secrets and That Twisty Killer Ending
	



			
			
	
						

									Courtesy of Peacock
	
					


							
		

	SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains major spoilers from “The Good Daughter,” now streaming on Peacock.

	For Sam and Charlie Quinn, the estranged sisters played by Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy in “The Good Daughter,” the truth was always going to set them free.

	Adapted by author Karin Slaughter from her own bestselling novel of the same name, the six-episode Peacock series gradually unravels a Southern Gothic family mystery. More than 20 years earlier, two masked gunmen broke into the Quinns’ rural Georgia home, murdering their mother, Gamma (Olivia Williams), and leaving both sisters with life-altering injuries. Rather than bonding them, the tragedy and a subsequent web of secrets drove the girls apart, culminating in a bitter falling-out a decade ago despite their shared career path. While Sam built a lucrative career in patent law in New York City, Charlie followed in her father Rusty’s (Brendan Gleeson) footsteps to practice criminal defense law in their shady fictional hometown of Pikeville.

	But when Charlie witnesses a tragic school shooting that leaves principal Douglas Pinkman (Kovar McClure) and a young student dead, Sam is pulled back to her old stomping grounds after Rusty is badly injured taking the suspect’s case. Forced to step in for her father despite not having very much experience as a defense attorney, Sam reluctantly agrees to represent Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), the pregnant teen who allegedly confessed to killing her principal and a much younger student.

	Over the course of the season, with the help of Charlie and her estranged husband Ben (Michael Dorman), Sam discovers that Kelly was merely a pawn used by Judith (Paula Malcomson), the kind teacher who looked after Charlie following Gamma’s death. Upon discovering her husband Douglas had abused and impregnated Kelly — and expected them all to raise the child together — Judith manipulated the unstable teen into bringing a gun to school, planning to kill Douglas and blame Kelly. But when Kelly hesitated to shoot, Judith seized the weapon, executing Douglas and accidentally killing another kid in the ensuing struggle.


	At the same time, the shooting resurfaces old memories for both Quinn sisters. As Sam digs deeper into the past, the truth of that tragic day finally comes to light: Charlie had been sexually assaulted by Zach Culpepper — one of Rusty’s most dangerous clients who owed him thousands in legal bills — and the brutal home invasion that resulted in Gamma’s murder had been orchestrated by Mason “Huck” Huckabee (Jake McDorman), a man with whom Charlie had a one-night stand right before the school shooting in the first episode.



	

					Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne 
									Courtesy of Mark Hill/PEACOCK
	



	Though Charlie had forced Rusty to keep her assault a secret for decades, confronting these buried traumas finally breaks down the walls threatening Charlie’s relationship with Sam — and her marriage to Ben. “It’s always really hard when we have things that we don’t like about ourselves, or things that we haven’t confronted about ourselves,” Fahy tells Variety. “That can be a really hard thing to communicate to someone else because when you operate out of a place of hurt, you do close yourself off from the people that you actually want to be closest to. I think that is true for the sisters and the beginning of the series, and then you have the payoff of watching them come through the other side of that and come back together.”

	In the conversation below, conducted separately, Byrne (also an executive producer) and Fahy discuss the “corrosive” nature of family secrets, why they believe Sam and Charlie are ultimately more alike than different — and whether that cathartic finale is truly the last we’ve seen of the Quinn sisters onscreen together.


	
		What intrigued each of you about how Sam and Charlie’s shared history informs their interactions in the present day?	

	Rose Byrne: The estrangement and the origin story of Sam returning home to face her personal truths was really intriguing. She had such fury and anger, which she speaks about in the show and in the book a lot, but [I was interested in] her coming to terms with her anger toward her father and his decisions that led them to this tragedy they find themselves in. I thought the nature of truth was also really interesting — [with] one person’s perspective then shifting to another and the tension of that, and the great suspenseful nature of the story. That genre has always been really fun to me, and something I hadn’t done for a long time, so it was fun to revisit those tropes.

	Meghann Fahy: Ultimately, the thing that really attracted me to the show is that, when you zoom out, it really is the story of confronting your grief and your trauma and the things that keep us at an arm’s length from the people that we love. It tells a story of coming out on the other side of that stronger and living more of a connected existence, and then drawing the people that you love closer to you as a result of having really faced yourself.


	
		The show plays with the idea that the sisters have different memories of the day their mother was killed — and there has been a sense of guilt and resentment under all of their interactions ever since. Why do you think Sam chose to leave Pikeville as soon as possible while Charlie decided to stay — and almost became trapped — in their hometown?	

	Byrne: Sam’s driven very much by her mother and her mother’s words of, “You have to leave. This town is corrupt. It’s rigged. It’s run by these people and you’ve got to get out.” Her sense of really pushing the daughters to leave to a bigger world, to a better place, to more opportunities, particularly as young women — I think that is her drive. The voice in her head is her mother’s voice, and she’s very much like her mother. She’s extremely bright; she’s very ambitious. I think the only way through life is to leave and to go somewhere where she can see like-minded people and be less oppressed and repressed in this town, which can be pretty challenging and pretty backward.

	Fahy: I don’t think Charlie wanted to leave her dad. I think that she wanted to follow in his footsteps in terms of doing the work that she had seen him do for their whole lives, and there’s something really interesting about that because Charlie and Sam obviously suffered in a big way as a result of what he did for a living and how that affected the family. There was something about Charlie that wanted to stay to rewrite the story or to take control of elements of the story that she didn’t feel that she had. And for her, the path to doing that was staying where it all happened.



	

					Meghann Fahy and Brendan Gleeson 
									Courtesy of Mark Hill/PEACOCK
	




	
		Meghann, Charlie notably only told her father about being raped on the day of Gamma’s killing. Did that secret inform your performance at all? Were there any little details that you added in to allude to that traumatic part of her history?	

	Fahy: Karin did a really good job of weaving that in. A lot of Charlie’s behavior, especially as it applies to her husband, Ben — at the beginning of the show, they’re not really together, but you sort of want them to be. But you understand why he is taking a step back, because the fact that she hasn’t processed any of this trauma that he doesn’t even know about is keeping him from really being with her, and it’s keeping her from really letting him in. That undercurrent is there the whole time, so I didn’t feel like I had to do anything special or extra to lace that in, because Karin did such a good job of building it in the relationships. You see Charlie suffering in her relationships, and you find out why much later, but I think if you watched the show from the beginning and you knew that, you would really be able to see that throughline in her and her behavior throughout the series.


	
		Rose, Charlie’s secret is obviously corrosive to her relationship with Sam, but why do you think Sam also struggles to be forthcoming with her own sister?	

	Byrne: I think it’s her disappointment in her sister after what she sacrificed for her. To your point, this secret is so corrosive to their relationship because Sam doesn’t know the truth. Her sister’s behavior is so triggering for Sam and so disappointing and so crushing when their mother had set this example of leaving and escaping, and I think her lack of compassion for her sister really is a great flaw in the character. Obviously, once she finds out the truth, she understands the whole perspective and also her anger. But that is another very specific trait in Sam that is really roadblocking her ability to have compassion and accept that her sister is not her.



	

									Courtesy of Mark Hill/PEACOCK
	





	
		Whether they were together or apart, Rusty clearly continued to have a hold on both of his daughters — so much so that they followed him into the same profession. Why do you think both of the Quinn daughters ended up practicing law, considering how their lives were left changed for the worst by their father’s insistence on representing criminals in Pikeville?	

	Fahy: The girls were raised in a house that was very intellectually driven. The scenes where you see Gamma teaching them, the way that she spoke to them — I always think it’s so funny when they’re in the store, and she’s giving Sam a lesson on how to really land saying “Fuck!,” and using her breath and stuff like that. That part of how they were raised is something that they both actually really like.

	Byrne: Sam’s law is patent law, so it’s so dry; it’s so unemotional, and it is so specific. I think she adores how benign it can be, and she thrives in the specificity of it, in the numbers of it. Whereas Charlie’s character, she feels so tied to her father. I think the trauma bond she has with her father and the secret they share — it’s very, very hard for her to leave that, and to leave what they’ve shared together in that sense.


	Fahy: For all of her father’s faults, he protected her when she needed him to. He kept the secret that she asked him to. I think she respected him, and Sam doesn’t in the same way, but then ultimately comes to feel that way about him towards the end.

	Byrne: It’s like that great Ram Dass saying: “If you think you’re enlightened, then go and spend a weekend with your parents.” I feel like that speaks really truth to everybody who’s alive and has parents who are alive. There’s just no relationship on Earth like it, and it is so powerful. You can think all the things you want about yourself until you’re back in front of whoever consists of your family. I feel like this is a really great examination of that, particularly with Samantha.

	Fahy: Sam and Charlie both wanting to go into the field of law is rooted ultimately in their respect for what they saw their father achieve, regardless of how it ultimately negatively affected everyone in the family and caused their mother to be killed. And that’s so awful, but I do think that, ultimately, they really love feeling like they’re helping people. I know that’s true for Charlie at least. That’s the thing she loves the most about what she does: helping kids that she feels like don’t have anybody else who wants to in the same way that she does.


	
		Meghann, you recorded a cover of Guns N’ Roses’ “Sweet Child O’ Mine” for the fifth episode, in which Sam and Charlie grieve Rusty’s death and go looking for an old photo in one of his old properties — where they uncover evidence about Huck’s involvement in Gamma’s death. How did that cover come about? Was there a particular reason that you chose that song?	

	Fahy: Our director, Steph Green, had found a version of the song that she really, really liked, and she knew that I sang, and she asked if I would be open to covering it. I, of course, was very excited by the idea. She wanted it to come after Episode 5 because she feels like some of the words, especially in the first verse, could be Charlie singing to Sam. I think the way that the episode ends where Charlie’s in the doorway and she’s calling for her sister the way that she did in the first episode — it’s like this callback to her being a child and standing in that same spot right before the worst thing happened. I like that the version that we did is a little bit haunting, a little bit stripped down.



	

									Courtesy of Mark Hill/PEACOCK
	




	
		Shortly after Rusty’s funeral, Sam, Charlie, and Ben discover that the two masked men who broke into the Quinn house decades earlier were Zack Culpepper and Huck, not Zack and his brother Daniel (as Charlie had been led to believe). Huck confesses that he had recruited Zack to attack Rusty in retaliation for Rusty defending the man accused of raping Huck’s sister. Can you each give voice to your characters’ internal dialogue after discovering that Huck had effectively caused the shooting of their mother and their own assaults?	

	Byrne: Karin Slaughter is so interesting, because she’s so ahead of the reader. She’s so ahead of her audience with her plots, but I do feel like Sam is that role too, and she’s a little bit ahead of the audience in her mind about what’s happening and she’s piecing it all together faster than everybody else. That was something I talked about a lot with Karin, so I tried to remember that in those scenes. I think she intuitively already knows all of this, and it’s catching up in real time as we’re watching it.

	Fahy: What’s so interesting about the show is it’s so nuanced in terms of who did what, who is guilty of what, and who was wrong, because Charlie did accuse the wrong person [Daniel] of assaulting her — and that person was killed. So in the moment that she realizes that, she feels incredibly guilty for having essentially been responsible for someone losing their life. But also, she was a kid, and she was confused, and she only had the information that was in front of her. I think that really speaks to the way that we process trauma. Sometimes, it’s really hard to zoom out and look at things from a different point of view when all you can feel is the trauma that your body is still in fight or flight.

	She’s unraveling all of that, feeling the guilt of that, feeling the anger of having been intimate with Huck, who is now a part of the worst day of her life. Ultimately, I think that Charlie finding out all of this is the thing that breaks her open, that ultimately allows her to come face to face with her truth. That is part of the catalyst to her being able to share that with Ben, which is what she needed to do so that they could really be together in a real way.

	Byrne: They say in the birth order, the eldest daughter is such a huge responsibility in a family, especially for a young girl. So to see her sister go through this trauma again and relive it again in front of her is really harrowing and makes her so wildly furious that I feel like that is another very specific thing she’s going through.


	
		As if Charlie weren’t dealing with enough, she discovers that Judith manipulated Kelly Wilson into killing Douglas.	

	Fahy: Judith was there the day that Charlie was assaulted in the woods. Charlie shows up to her door, and Judith takes her in. After that, Judith continues to take care of her in school. She sticks up for Charlie when she’s being bullied. For Charlie, feeling safe with anybody is a tall order. So for her to come to the realization that a person that she really trusted and felt looked after by could have done something so horrible — I think she was a cocktail of emotions, but there was a real, real sadness and heartbreak in there when Charlie realized that Judith really was the one who orchestrated the killings.


	
		Karin Slaughter actually wrote a “digital short” prequel to “The Good Daughter” called “Last Breath” in which a younger Charlie takes on a high-stakes case involving a motherless teenager. Since nothing in success is really ever limited these days, have any of you had conversations about what a second season of “The Good Daughter” could look like, or did you always envision this adaptation as a one-and-done series?	

	Byrne: That’s so cool. I didn’t know that.

	Fahy: Because the novel is so beautifully written, it felt complete to me — and the show felt complete to me, too. I don’t think I ever really pictured it as being ongoing. But that being said, Charlie is one of my most cherished characters that I’ve ever been able to play, so she’ll stay with me for a long time. I would be very curious to know what she would be getting up to and what her life would be like after having gone through everything that she goes through.

	Byrne: We felt it was pretty contained within the pages of what we were doing, but I’ve also been around so long that now I don’t know what anywhere will lead to anywhere anymore. So “anything can happen” is really my motto now in this business, because you just never know how things will shake out. I always try to keep an open mind, but it feels like the story we were meant to tell was the one we’ve told.




	

					Meghann Fahy and Michael Dorman 
									Mark Hill/PEACOCK
	



	
		Charlie mentions at the end of the finale that she and Ben are moving to Atlanta, and Sam will presumably go back to New York while maintaining a much healthier relationship with her younger sister going forward. What do you imagine their respective lives will look like after the screen cuts to black?	

	Byrne: Maybe they go to a private island and have a mojito. I’m being silly, but I’m kind of not. They deserve a drink! They should talk about the weather for a few weeks, and keep it really light. Not the news — just the weather, what they’re going to have for dinner. That’s what I would like: for them to be a little bored, a little quiet, just relaxed.

	Fahy: I hope that Charlie finds real comfort and peace. Another thing that I really, really love about the character of Ben, played by Michael Dorman — we were so lucky to have him because his energy is so unique and loving and understanding. I think we don’t show a lot of relationships like Charlie and Ben where the person is given space to figure themselves out, and Ben’s not punishing her for it. He’s loving her through it while also having his own boundary.

	To see them come back together after having given each other that space, and for him to really hold all of Charlie’s truth and say, “I’m still here,” is so hopeful and nice. We should show more of that because if you’re lucky enough to be in a really healthy relationship, that’s what you would hope would be true for anybody. So I loved that the conflict was never really between the two of them. It was just the work Charlie had to do, and he allowed her to do that. So I hope that after “The Good Daughter,” Charlie and Ben are super happy in Atlanta and that they’re just finally really enjoying each other.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘The Good Daughter’ Stars Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy on Playing Sisters With Secrets and That Twisty Killer Ending

body:
Dawn Greenhalgh, a veteran Canadian actress of stage, film and television, died Nov. 6 in Toronto. She was 93.

	Born in Shanghai, China, she spent her childhood with her family in a Japanese prisoner of war camp, where she discovered a love for music, theater and dance. Greenhalgh moved to Canada with only a guardian at the age of 14, attending Montreal High School and beginning her performing career.


	In 1953, at 19 years old, she became a founding member of Canada’s Stratford Festival. She went on to become a founding member of the Neptune Theatre in Halifax and Theatre Plus in Toronto. She performed on stages around the world and in New York studied with Uta Haagen, Herbert Berghof and Mira Rostova. 
	

	Greenhalgh’s film roles included Sofia Coppola‘s “The Virgin Suicides” and David Cronenberg’s “Map to the Stars.” She also worked with her daughter, Megan Follows, in the popular Canadian series “Anne of Green Gables.” Other television appearances included “Five Days at Memorial,” “Saving Hope” and “La Femme Nikita.” She voiced Queen Celeste, Babar the elephant’s wife, on the animated series “Babar.”

	With the Stratford Festival, she performed in plays including “All’s Well That Ends Well” with Alec Guinness, “Antony and Cleopatra” and “Love’s Labour’s Lost.”

	“Dawn Greenhalgh was a powerhouse, a dynamic, brilliant actress,” Stratford Festival Artistic Director Antoni Cimolino wrote on Instagram. “As an extraordinary artist she could be both charming and unsettling. It was a pleasure to hear her perspective on plays and productions as it was informed by a lifetime of wide experience, a sparkling intellect and an independent, free thinking mind.”
	

	She is survived by her children Edwina Follows; Laurence Follows; Samantha Follows and Megan Follows, six grandchildren and two step-grandchildren.

schema.headline: Dawn Greenhalgh, Canadian Stage Veteran Who Voiced the Queen in ‘Babar,’ Dies at 93

title: ‘Club Kid’ Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra on Capturing Intimate and Authentic New York Moments
description: Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra enjoys working with directors who also act in their films. This year alone, his work includes “The Invite” with
body:
Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra enjoys working with directors who also act in their films. This year alone, his work includes “The Invite” with director and actor Olivia Wilde, as well as teaming up with Jordan Firstman on A24’s “Club Kid,” in which Firstman directs and stars.

	Newport-Berra (Variety’s 10 Artisans to Watch 2026) says, “I tend to enjoy working with actor-directors because we get this dynamic experience on set where they get to direct the film both from outside and from within during the scene, which I think is a special opportunity for a director to be able to be inside the scene, guiding it as it’s happening.”
	

	While “The Invite” challenged him to work with Wilde to be creative within a single space, “Club Kid” — which opens this weekend — is set in New York City. The film stars Firstman, Cara Delevingne, Diego Calva, Kirby Howell-Baptiste and Reggie Absolom. It follows a queer party promoter who has long outgrown his time on the scene. However, his life is upended when he suddenly meets the 10-year-old son (Absolom) he never knew he had, forcing him to grapple with the kind of life he wants to lead. Over time, Peter slowly begins to adjust to life with Arlo, and in one memorable scene, the pair sit at a piano as Newport-Berra’s camera slowly zooms out to capture a perfect evening and moment.



	

	



	Newport-Berra shares, “Originally, we were going to shoot a whole montage of them spending a day together that would culminate in this moment.” However, time, budget and production priorities led to the montage being scrapped and the focus shifted to moving the piano up a flight of stairs. Newport-Berra recalls that after shooting in the apartment for a few weeks, the crew started feeling claustrophobic. “We were like, ‘What if we were looking at the apartment from this window or from that roof?’” The production team scouted until they found a building willing to let them shoot on the roof.
	

	He continues, “We had this amazing zoom-out shot timed perfectly with a dolly shot inside. It starts with a dolly pulling out, which we lit and set up probably an hour or two before we were ready to shoot so we could get the perfect light. We let them rehearse and play around. There were two cameras rolling at the same time. The camera outside doesn’t see the camera inside because it’s just off the window, hidden behind it. As the dolly camera pulls out, the other camera zooms out, keeping itself out of the shot so we could time everything perfectly to the exact moment of sunset. It became this really magical moment.”

	Overall, Newport-Berra appreciated working with Firstman, noting that they had shotlisted the entire film beforehand. “But we were keen to take the temperature on set and figure out what the moment needed. Sometimes it was very clear to us that we wanted a very intimate, simple handheld camera, where I could just be between them — the three of us in the room. Other times, the camera needed to be locked off and observing the pair from a distance. The nuance of everything very much came from being in the moment together in the room.”



	

	



	As for capturing New York, Newport-Berra felt confident he could help portray an authentic version of the city. He started his career there, working on indie films, student projects and music videos. “I know the city very well. I lived there for over a decade and really fell in love with it.” He adds that he and Firstman wanted to make “Club Kid” feel like an iconic, nostalgic New York movie, but with a fresh perspective. Their familiarity with the city helped immensely, as did Newport-Berra’s connections with local crew members that dated back to his student days.

	“It was a very small movie,” he recalls. “We were all carrying camera cases upstairs, cramming into the back of a van to get from one location to another, loading film on the sidewalk and politely asking random bystanders to move out of the way so we could steal a shot.” He concludes, “It was very much a New York indie movie and I love that. I’m proud we got to make that movie there.”

schema.headline: ‘Club Kid’ Cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra on Capturing Intimate and Authentic New York Moments

title: Box Office: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Leads With $6.7 Million on Opening Day, ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Struggling With $2.2 Million on Friday
description: “Ebenezer,” an adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge, led the box office on Friday with $6.7 million on opening day.
body:
“Ebenezer,” an adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge, led the box office on Friday with $6.7 million on opening day.

	The PG-13 take on the Charles Dickens classic is projected to earn $18 million to $20 million from 3,535 North American theaters in its opening weekend. “Ebenezer” should bring in another $20 million overseas for a global tally around $38 million to $40 million. That would represent a solid start because Paramount spent a modest $38 million to produce the film. Audiences awarded the movie an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. Directed by Ti West, known for the “X” horror trilogy, “Ebenezer” spins the oft-told tale of the curmudgeonly businessman who is visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future.
	

	“Ebenezer” is notable as Depp’s first major movie in eight years, since 2018’s “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald.” Warner Bros. fired him from the “Harry Potter” spinoff series in 2020 after he lost a libel case against the British tabloid The Sun, which called the actor a “wife beater.” Depp won a subsequent defamation trial in the U.S. against his ex-wife Amber Heard, who accused him of domestic abuse. As Hollywood kept a distance, Depp appeared in underseen indies like the 2020 drama “Minamata” and the 2023 period piece “Jeanne du Barry” and he directed the 2024 biopic “Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness.”

	Another newcomer, Sony’s action thriller “Ghost Soldier,” starring Jim Caviezel as a former American Special Forces soldier, grossed $1.5 million from 2,558 locations on Friday. It’s expected to generate $4.9 million during the traditional weekend and $8 million over its first five days of release. It was produced for $18 million.
	

	This weekend’s other new release, Amazon MGM’s “How to Rob a Bank,” is fizzling with $2.2 million from 2,810 theaters on Friday. The heist comedy, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, is pacing to open to just $4.75 million. That’s not promising considering the studio produced the movie for more than $40 million, and theater owners keep about half of ticket sales. David Leitch directed the R-rated caper, which follows a crew of social media-savvy bank robbers who broadcast their daring heists, unaware their viral fame has caught the attention of the feds. “How to Rob a Bank” landed a “B-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls and tepid 33% from critics on Rotten Tomatoes.

	“How to Rob a Bank” placed third on Friday, but it’s bracing for No. 7 on weekend box office charts behind several holdovers, including Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat” and Gkids’ “Godzilla Minus Zero.” At No. 2, “The Cat in the Hat” brought in $2.2 million on Friday and looks to generate $10 million by Sunday, a 50% decline from its debut. Those ticket sales would take the domestic total to $36.7 million, a weak tally against a $92 million budget. “Godzilla Minus Zero” wasn’t far behind with $2.1 million on Friday. The kaiju sequel should collect $7.5 million in its second weekend, a harsh 75% drop from its opening. Still, “Godzilla Minus Zero” has been a hit in North America. Those returns will bring the Stateside haul to $48.1 million.

schema.headline: Box Office: Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Leads With $6.7 Million on Opening Day, ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Struggling With $2.2 Million on Friday

title: Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced His Second Mid-Show Departure
description:
Nov 14, 2026 11:07am PT	
	

	
		Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced Hi
body:
Nov 14, 2026 11:07am PT	
	

	
		Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced His Second Mid-Show Departure
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty Images for Journey
	

		
	
				


	Journey drummer Deen Castronovo is out of the band, the group announced Friday, due to health issues that caused him to have to drop out of two shows mid-concert in the space of just over a month, the latest of which was Tuesday night in Boston. 

	After he was replaced by his drum tech as an emergency fill-in partway through the Tuesday Boston show, the band performed Thursday night in Cleveland with a new drummer, Steve Murphy. On Friday, the group finally addressed the issue in a statement and said that Murphy would be stepping into Castronovo’s shoes as their full-time drummer going forward.

	The band’s social media post read: “Dear Friends… After careful consideration and an extensive year of touring, our talented, longtime drummer Deen Castronovo has decided to step away to focus on personal health matters that require his attention. He has our full support during this time and extends his heartfelt thanks to the fans for the love, encouragement, and kindness he has received. Native New Yorker Steve Murphy, who comes to us from working with bands such as Alan Parsons Project, Trans Siberian Orchestra, Christopher Cross and Jack Bruce, will be joining us for the remainder of November. We look forward to continuing to share unforgettable nights of music with all of you.”

	The post did not include any photos of Castronovo, but did include shots of Murphy celebrating his first show with the band Thursday.

	The message was also shared on Castronovo’s personal Facebook page. The drummer did not offer any additional comment of his own beyond the band’s statement, but none might have been expected, as he has previously noted he leaves it to someone else to oversee his social media accounts.

	Castronovo, 62, who joined Journey in 1998, had to leave Tuesday’s show in Boston 12 songs into the show, according to reports posted on Setlists.fm. He was replaced for the rest of the truncated set by a fill-in, his drum tech, Steve Toomey, just as he had been a month earlier under similar circumstances in Tulsa. The length of Tuesday’s show was cut down from the usual 29 or so songs to 20, with eight songs following Castronovo’s stage departure. 


	On Oct. 8 in Oklahoma, he left the stage after just two songs and was hospitalized; Toomey also completed the show that night. Whatever was ailing Castronovo was not explained to the public. But at that time the band said publicly that he quickly bounced back and was in fighting trim to resume the tour. Castronovo indeed played their next show on Oct. 10 without incident, as he did all the subsequent shows through Nov. 7, before apparently falling ill again mid-show Tuesday.

	Castronovo joined Journey in 1998 to replace original drummer Steve Smith. He was forced out of the group in 2015 after being charged with assaulting a woman, and was replaced at that time by Omar Hakim. He subsequently had nine charges dismissed and pleaded guilty to six others, receiving a suspended sentence. He came back to rejoin the Journey lineup in 2021, after performing with guitarist Neal Schon on a side-project tour in 2019.


	In 2023, the drummer explained his perseonal journey in and out of Journey — and back in — in an interview with Ultimate Classic Rock. “I had to take some time off and, pardon my language, get my shit together. I was a mess, and it was horrible what happened. But today, I’m doing great, clean and sober, working hard, doing what I need to do – and I put God first, family second. My job is third, where before it was all the other way around: ‘I want to be a rocker, I want to play music and I want to party,’ and everything was on the back burner – everything else, which is really sad. … I was so wrapped up in drugs and alcohol; family was way down the line. That was heartbreaking. But here I am today, and family is most important, and my job is great. I love what I do with Journey and I love what I do with Revolution Saints, but the beautiful thing is what I learned the most, being in treatment, is that if it all went away, you know what? I’m still all right. … I love playing, but if it was all to go away tomorrow, God bless, man. Life goes on, and I’m OK with myself. I’m comfortable in my skin.”
	

	There are eight shows left on Journey’s 2026 tour, including a Saturday night stop in Greenville, before the band wraps up the touring year Nov. 28 in San Francisco. Journey had previously announced this as part of a farewell tour, but Schon said recently that the long goodbye was going so well, they had plans to proceed indefinitely.

	“Your love, energy and passion for this music have reminded us how much we still share and how much this journey means to all of us,” Schon wrote. “What began as ‘The Final Frontier’ now feels more like ‘The Long Goodbye.’ We’re letting our hearts — and the connection we feel with you every night — help guide what comes next.”


	
		More from Variety

title: Shane Gillis Was Surprised by ‘SNL’ Monologue Backlash and Says He Doesn’t ‘Have a Problem’ With How Women Dress at the Gym
description:
Shane Gillis is reflecting on his “Saturday Night Live” monologue about women’s gym attire that drew controversy.

	On the Oct. 10 episode this sea
body:
Shane Gillis is reflecting on his “Saturday Night Live” monologue about women’s gym attire that drew controversy.

	On the Oct. 10 episode this season, the comedian’s opening monologue included jokes about how women “dress like whores now” at the gym, which inspired a wave of criticism on social media. Gillis revealed on the Nov. 13 episode of the “Joe Rogan Experience” that he was surprised by the blowback.


	“The funniest part was, I was going in going — they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad,’” he said. “The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for fucking 10 minutes. That’s it.’”
	

	He also said that he thinks the reaction “obviously had a lot to do with the climate” and, with regard to the gym attire, “for the record, [I] don’t have a problem with it.”

	Gillis also clarified that “Saturday Night Live” gave no feedback about the joke ahead of time.

	“Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don’t approve it. I mean, they could shut it down,” he said to Rogan. “They could, but you don’t write your set and give it to them. Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them.”

	The original joke ignited criticism online and even a response from Inde Navarrette during her “SNL” monologue.

	“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said in the monologue. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe it. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts? Those neon, they’re like artificial bait-colored. And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combined at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.”
	

	Watch Gillis talk about the controversy on Rogan’s show below.

description:

body:
Illinois Town Evacuated
                          Bomb Found At Highly Combustible Industrial Plant
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 14, 2026
                            6:55 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A bomb was discovered at a highly combustible industrial plant as authorities ordered the evacuation of everyone within a possible mile-wide blast radius.
      
    
            It all went down in suburban Peoria, Illinois, after Peoria police found a suspicious package by the BioUrja ethanol plant Friday afternoon at around 2 PM ... CBS News reported.
      
    
            Deeming the threat to be "credible," an evacuation order for residents within a one-mile blast radius from the plant was issued by cops ... with a shelter set up at Manual Academy.
      

            Hours later ... the bomb was eventually "rendered safe" around 9 PM that night ... according to Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon.
      
    
            However, cops are still combing the area for any additional devices.
      
    
            Dixon stressed to reporters ... "The area of BioUrja has not been rendered safe, just the package that was on site. It's a large facility, there's going to be an exhaustive search."
      
    
            Peoria Mayor Rita Ali claimed in an interview with WMBD News that the bomb's location was alarming given how combustible the ethanol plant is.

            Brandi Glanville said she is still left with questions after a black mass was removed from her face during a recent surgery ... and says that there's even more buried under the surface.
      
    
            On yesterday's episode of "Brandi Glanville Unfiltered" ... Brandi told her listeners that only one of several black masses was removed ... and that "we're not sure what that is yet."
      
    
            She also said that she was unable to go to her close friend Markee M. Hasche's funeral due to fluid in her ears.
      

            She admitted ... "I keep on thinking and talking myself into this crazy thing like, 'Oh my god, people hate me. Mark's family hates me.' But I had so much fluid in my ears, it just wasn't possible. Like, I couldn't fly. I couldn't drive."
      
    
            Brandi also detailed her son Mason's heartbreaking reaction to her diagnosis.

I go, 'Mason, I want to fall in love again. I don't want to sit home every night and be a recluse.'"
      
    
            We reported earlier ... Brandi -- who suffers from highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, Coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever), Demodex dermatitis, and mononucleosis -- had the pearl-sized mass removed in October.
      
    
            The mass is currently undergoing testing.

            Former L.A. Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa experienced something all Angelenos can relate to ... having the car that was meant to pick you up at LAX moved due to their no-waiting policy.
